chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Position Sizing Is the Real Edge

lessons.title: Case Study: How Overleveraged Nifty Options Sizing Wipes Out a Winning System

children.text: Karthik is a 29-year-old engineer in Bengaluru who spent a year backtesting a weekly options-selling system before ever risking real money. The system was genuinely good. It had a real, measurable, positive edge every week it ran. It still cost him five months of gains in a single trading session. This case study walks through exactly what happened, using nothing more than the tools built in this chapter's first two lessons: probability, payoff ratio, bankroll and expectancy.
The System: A Genuine, Modest Edge

Karthik's system sold out-of-the-money Nifty weekly strangles every Thursday, with a fixed stop-loss of ₹22,000 per lot if the position moved against him. Backtested over three years of expiries, it looked like this:

stats.label: Avg win
stats.context: Per lot, most weeks expire quietly

stats.label: Avg loss
stats.context: Per lot, roughly 2.4x the average win

children.text: Using the formula from the previous lesson, E(R) = p·b − q = (0.78 × 0.41) − 0.22 ≈ +0.10R. A modest but real positive edge, exactly the profile most retail premium-selling systems have: they win often, by a little, and occasionally lose by a lot more. Nothing about this system was fraudulent or curve-fitted. It genuinely made money on average, week after week.

Karthik started with ₹10,00,000 in trading capital and one lot per week. A planned loss of ₹22,000 on one lot was 2.2% of his bankroll, a sensible size by any standard sizing rule this course will cover. For eight weeks, this is exactly how he traded.

body.text: Notice what actually changed between Week 8 and Week 22: not the system, not the backtested edge, not even the market regime. What changed was that Karthik kept adding lots because "it had been working," the same reasoning Trader C used to justify a 30% bet size in Lesson 1. Position size grew with his confidence, not with any recalculation against his current bankroll.

children.text: The Day the Tail Showed Up

In Week 23, an unexpected macro headline hit the market shortly after the open. Nifty moved sharply in one direction, with almost no two-way trade to absorb the move. This is illustrative price action built to show the shape of the risk, not an actual historical NSE session:

body.title: Illustrative Nifty price action into the tail event (not actual historical data)

children.text: A stop-loss on a short option is a promise, not a guarantee. It only fills at the intended price if someone is willing to take the other side there. In a fast, one-directional move, option premiums can reprice far faster than the underlying, and a seller trying to exit finds the price has gapped well past the planned stop before the order fills. Karthik's ₹22,000-per-lot planned stop became roughly ₹88,000 per lot by the time he was actually out, a four-times overshoot driven entirely by slippage in a market with no willing buyer at his stop level.

body.title: Size the damage
body.prompt: Karthik's account fell from ₹13,50,000 to ₹9,10,000 in one session. What was the percentage drawdown?
body.explanation: (₹13,50,000 − ₹9,10,000) ÷ ₹13,50,000 ≈ 32.6%. Getting back to ₹13,50,000 from ₹9,10,000 now requires a gain of roughly 48%, on a system whose backtested edge was only about +0.10R per trade.

children.text: What One Lot Would Have Looked Like

The tail event itself was outside Karthik's control. The size of the position it hit was entirely inside his control. Compare what the identical event would have done to an account still sized at one lot against his current ₹13,50,000 bankroll.

body.text: This system's edge was real throughout. E(R) never turned negative. The failure was entirely a sizing failure: increasing lots as a reward for a winning streak, without re-checking that size against current capital or against the fact that a premium-selling system's worst loss is not well described by its "typical" stop-loss at all. Chapter 5 returns to this exact problem when it covers fat tails and why Kelly's own assumptions need adjusting for strategies like this one.

body.title: Find the mistake, before it happens
body.scenario: Rewind to Week 13, the moment Karthik decided to scale from 1 lot to 3 lots after a good run.
body.prompt: What question should he have asked himself before increasing size, based on the tools from this chapter, and what would a disciplined answer have looked like?
body.modelAnswer: He should have asked: "What fraction of my current capital does this new position size risk, and is that fraction still sensible given what I know about this system's worst-case loss, not just its typical stop-loss?" A disciplined answer would recalculate the risk fraction every time size changes, rather than increasing lots simply because recent results were good. It would also treat the ₹22,000 backtested average loss as a floor, not a ceiling, since option-selling systems are known to have losses that occasionally exceed the typical stop by several times once slippage in a fast market is accounted for.

body.title: What actually went wrong
body.question: What was the real cause of Karthik's five-month drawdown?
options: His system's expectancy, E(R), was negative all along
He scaled position size up with a winning streak, without resizing against current bankroll or accounting for tail risk
Nifty options are always too risky to sell for premium
His win rate of 78% was too low to be a real edge
body.explanation: E(R) stayed positive at roughly +0.10R throughout. The problem was pure position sizing: lot count grew with confidence rather than with a recalculated risk fraction, and the sizing plan never accounted for the fact that a short-option system's worst loss is far larger than its typical loss.

points: A system can have a genuine, backtested positive edge and still destroy an account. Edge and sizing are separate failure points.
Increasing position size because a system "has been working" is the same mistake as choosing an oversized bet fraction from Lesson 1, just spread across months instead of one simulation.
A stop-loss on a short option position is not a guaranteed exit price. In a fast, one-directional move, the actual loss can be several times the planned stop due to slippage.
Position size should be recalculated against current bankroll every time it changes, not increased as a reward for recent wins.
The same tail event that cost 32.6% of capital at 5 lots would have cost about 6.5% at 1 lot. Sizing decides how survivable an unavoidable bad day is.
